summary.text: Expanding the product identifies the normalized coefficient with an alternating sum of reciprocal-factorial weights of strict partitions; a transport that repeatedly lowers the bottom of the top consecutive run shows the weight for \(j-1\) parts is at most \(9/10\) of that for \(j\) parts, using recursive majorants, finite rational bounds for the small cases, and a geometrically decreasing tail. Hence the alternating sum has sign \((-1)^m\), where \(m\) is the largest index with \(m(m+1)/2\le n\), and this index changes from \(n-1\) to \(n\) exactly when \(n\) is triangular.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_k=1+2+\cdots+k=\frac{k(k+1)}2,\qquad T_0=0.
\]
For a finite set \(X\) of positive integers, put
\[
 |X|=\text{its cardinality},\qquad \sigma(X)=\sum_{x\in X}x,
 \qquad P(X)=\prod_{x\in X}x!.
\]
Thus finite sets of positive integers are the same thing as strict partitions. For \(j,s,n\geq0\), let
\[
 \mathcal S(j,s,n)=\{X:|X|=j,\ \sigma(X)=n,\ x\geq s\text{ for every }x\in X\},
\]
and write
\[
 e_j(n)=\sum_{X\in\mathcal S(j,1,n)}\frac1{P(X)}.
\]
All these sums are finite.

We shall prove first that, whenever \(T_j\leq n\) and \(j\geq2\),
\[
 e_{j-1}(n)\leq \frac9{10}e_j(n). \tag{1}
\]
This is the main estimate. In particular, because \(e_j(n)>0\) under these hypotheses, it implies
\[
 e_{j-1}(n)<e_j(n). \tag{2}
\]
After proving (1), the sign assertion follows from a short alternating-sum argument.

## 1. A sum-lowering operation on strict partitions

For a nonempty finite set \(X\), let
\[
 M(X)=\max X.
\]
Let \(\tau(X)\) be the bottom of the terminal consecutive run in \(X\): it is the least \(t\in X\) such that every integer from \(t\) through \(M(X)\) belongs to \(X\). Thus
\[
 [\tau(X),M(X)]\cap\mathbb N\subseteq X,
\]
and, if \(\tau(X)>0\), then \(\tau(X)-1\notin X\).

Define
\[
 \rho(X)=\bigl(X\setminus\{\tau(X)\}\bigr)\cup\{\tau(X)-1\}
\]
for nonempty \(X\), and put \(\rho(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). Whenever \(\tau(X)\geq1\), the new element is not already in the set, so
\[
 |\rho(X)|=|X|,
 \qquad \sigma(\rho(X))=\sigma(X)-1. \tag{3}
\]
Moreover, if every element of \(X\) is at least \(S\) and \(\tau(X)\geq S+1\), then every element of \(\rho(X)\) is still at least \(S\).

We need a precise description of the inverse branches of \(\rho\). For nonempty \(X\), define
\[
 A(X)=\bigl(X\setminus\{M(X)\}\bigr)\cup\{M(X)+1\}, \tag{4}
\]
and, when \(\tau(X)-2\in X\), define
\[
 B(X)=\bigl(X\setminus\{\tau(X)-2\}\bigr)\cup\{\tau(X)-1\}. \tag{5}
\]
Suppose \(S\geq1\), all elements of \(X\) are at least \(S\), and \(Z\ne\varnothing\) satisfies \(\rho(Z)=X\). Then all elements of \(Z\) are at least \(S\), \(\tau(Z)\geq S+1\), and exactly one of the following possibilities holds:

* \(Z=A(X)\);
* \(\tau(X)-2\in X\) and \(Z=B(X)\).

Here is the proof. Put \(u=\tau(Z)\). From the definition,
\[
 X=\{u-1\}\cup(Z\setminus\{u\}), \qquad
 Z=\{u\}\cup(X\setminus\{u-1\}). \tag{6}
\]
If \(u-1=M(X)\), (6) gives \(Z=A(X)\). Otherwise \(u-1<M(X)\). Since all elements from \(u\) to \(M(Z)\) lie in \(Z\), all elements from \(u+1\) to the common maximum lie in \(X\), while \(u\notin X\). Hence the terminal run of \(X\) begins at \(u+1\). Thus \(\tau(X)=u+1\), the element \(u-1=\tau(X)-2\) belongs to \(X\), and (6) gives \(Z=B(X)\).

The parameters and factorial weights on these branches are especially simple:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &M(A(X))=M(X)+1, &&\tau(A(X))=M(X)+1,
 &&\frac{P(X)}{P(A(X))}=\frac1{M(X)+1}; \tag{7}\\
 &M(B(X))=M(X), &&\tau(B(X))=\tau(X)-1,
 &&\frac{P(X)}{P(B(X))}=\frac1{\tau(X)-1}. \tag{8}
 \end{aligned}
\]
In the second line the branch condition forces \(\tau(X)\geq S+2\). The two candidate preimages are distinct, since \(A(X)\) contains \(M(X)+1\), whereas \(B(X)\) does not.

## 2. Weighted fibers and their recursive majorant

For \(S\geq1\), a nonempty set \(X\) whose elements are at least \(S\), and \(k\geq0\), define the weighted \(k\)-step fiber
\[
 f_k(X;S)=\sum_{\substack{Y:\,\rho^k(Y)=X\\ y\geq S\ (y\in Y)}}\frac{P(X)}{P(Y)}. \tag{9}
\]
One may harmlessly impose the finite upper bound
\(y\leq \sigma(X)+k\), since (3) implies \(\sigma(Y)=\sigma(X)+k\) for every relevant nonempty fiber element. Thus (9) is a finite sum.

The inverse-branch description and (7)–(8) give
\[
 f_{k+1}(X;S)\leq
 \frac{f_k(A(X);S)}{M(X)+1}
 +\begin{cases}
 \dfrac{f_k(B(X);S)}{\tau(X)-1},&\tau(X)-2\in X,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases} \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, split a \((k+1)\)-step fiber according to its first one-step preimage. Fibers belonging to distinct first preimages are disjoint, and
\[
 \frac{P(X)}{P(Y)}= rac{P(X)}{P(X_1)}\frac{P(X_1)}{P(Y)}.
\]
For \(k=0\), clearly \(f_0(X;S)\leq1\).

We encode (10) by a numerical recursion. For \(S,k,t,M\in\mathbb N\), define nonnegative rational numbers \(F_S(k,t,M)\) by
\[
 F_S(0,t,M)=1, \tag{11}
\]
\[
 F_S(k+1,t,M)=
 \frac{F_S(k,M+1,M+1)}{M+1}
 +\begin{cases}
 \dfrac{F_S(k,t-1,M)}{t-1},&S+2\leq t,\\
 0,&S+2>t.
 \end{cases} \tag{12}
\]
Induction using (7), (8), and (10) proves
\[
 f_k(X;S)\leq F_S(k,\tau(X),M(X)). \tag{13}
\]
The first term in (12) is the \(A\)-branch and the second is the possible \(B\)-branch. Notice that (12) deliberately includes the \(B\)-branch whenever its elementary parameter restrictions allow it, whether or not an actual set realizing that branch exists; hence it is a relaxed majorant.

## 3. Uniform estimates for the recursion \(F\)

We next establish the numerical estimate needed later:
\[
 \sum_{s=1}^{t-2}s!F_{s+1}(s,t,M)\leq\frac9{10}
 \quad(t\leq M), \tag{14}
\]
and the special estimate
\[
 \sum_{s=1}^{j-1}s!F_{s+1}(s,s+1,j)\leq\frac9{10}. \tag{15}
\]
Empty ranges are interpreted as zero.

We give all the majorants and reductions used to prove these bounds. Write
\[
 D(a,b)=a(a-1)\cdots(a-b+1),\qquad D(a,0)=1
\]
for the descending factorial. Define
\[
 c_S(b,m)=\frac1{D(\max\{m-1,S+b\},b)},
 \qquad z_S(b)=\frac1{D(S+b,b)}. \tag{16}
\]
Define three recursive families \(R,I,L\) by
\[
 R_S(0,b,m)=c_S(b,m), \tag{17}
\]
\[
 R_S(r+1,b,m)=R_S(r,b+1,m)
 +c_S(b,m)\frac{R_S(r,0,m+1)}{m+1}; \tag{18}
\]
\[
 I_S(0,b,t,m)=\frac1{D(t-1,b)}, \tag{19}
\]
\[
 I_S(r+1,b,t,m)=
 \begin{cases}I_S(r,b+1,t,m),&S+1\leq t-(b+1),\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
 +\frac1{D(t-1,b)}\frac{R_S(r,0,m+1)}{m+1}; \tag{20}
\]
and
\[
 L_S(0,b,q)=z_S(b), \tag{21}
\]
\[
 L_S(r+1,b,q)=L_S(r,b+1,q)
 +z_S(b)\frac{L_S(r,0,q)}{q+1}. \tag{22}
\]
All these quantities are nonnegative.

The elementary monotonicity of descending factorials gives the following comparisons. They follow by induction on the recursion depth; we state the hypotheses because they explain every later substitution:

1. If \(S\leq m\leq T+b\), \(m\leq M'\), and, when \(b\geq1\), \(S+1\leq T\), then
\[
 \frac{F_S(k,T,M')}{D(T+b-1,b)}\leq R_S(k,b,m). \tag{23}
\]
For the branch lowering \(T\), use
\[
 D(T+b-2,b+1)=(T-1)D(T+b-1,b),
\]
which supplies exactly the divisor \(T-1\) in (12). For the branch raising the maximum, apply the induction hypothesis with \(b=0\) and \(m+1\), then use \(m+1\leq M'+1\). This gives (18).

2. If \(S\leq m\leq M'\), and, for \(b\geq1\), \(S+1\leq t-b\), then
\[
 \frac{F_S(k,t-b,M')}{D(t-1,b)}\leq I_S(k,b,t,m). \tag{24}
\]
The lowering branch increments \(b\), while the maximum-raising branch is bounded by (23), exactly producing (20).

3. If \(q\leq m\), then
\[
 R_S(r,b,m)\leq L_S(r,b,q). \tag{25}
\]
Also, under the same side condition as in (24),
\[
 I_S(r,b,t,m)\leq L_S(r,b,q). \tag{26}
\]
These follow from
\(c_S(b,m)\leq z_S(b)\), the induction hypotheses, and
\(1/(m+1)\leq1/(q+1)\).

For the large-\(s\) tail we use simpler power bounds. Since each of the \(b\) factors in \(D(S+b,b)\) is at least \(S+1\),
\[
 z_S(b)\leq\frac1{(S+1)^b},
 \qquad c_S(b,m)\leq\frac1{(S+1)^b}. \tag{27}
\]
Induction in (18) and (20), bounding both recursive summands by equal powers, gives
\[
 R_S(r,b,m)\leq\frac{2^r}{(S+1)^{r+b}}\quad(S\leq m), \tag{28}
\]
\[
 I_S(r,b,t,m)\leq\frac{2^r}{(S+1)^{r+b}} \tag{29}
\]
under the side conditions already stated. The factor \(2\) at each step simply accounts for the two nonnegative branches.

Put
\[
 u_s=\frac{s!\,2^s}{(s+2)^s}. \tag{30}
\]
We shall use
\[
 5u_{s+1}\leq4u_s. \tag{31}
\]
For completeness, one way to prove (31) is to use, for \(x\geq0\),
\[
 x^{r+2}+r x^{r+1}+\frac{r(r-1)}2x^r\leq x^2(x+1)^r. \tag{32}
\]
This is proved by induction on \(r\): multiply the inequality for \(r\) by \(x+1\), expand, and discard the nonnegative excess term. Taking \(x=s+2\) and rearranging (32) yields
\[
 5(s+1)(s+2)^s\leq2(s+3)^{s+1},
\]
which, after inserting the factorial and power-of-two factors, is precisely (31). Consequently, summing the geometric domination \(u_{s+r}\leq(4/5)^r u_s\),
\[
 \sum_{r=a}^{N}u_r\leq5u_a. \tag{33}
\]

It remains only a small exact rational computation. Define
\[
 G(t)=\sum_{s=1}^{t-2}s!I_{s+1}(s,0,t,t), \tag{34}
\]
\[
 G_0(j)=\sum_{s=1}^{j-1}
 \frac{s!}{j+1}R_{s+1}(s-1,0,j+1), \tag{35}
\]
\[
 C_1=\sum_{s=1}^{12}s!L_{s+1}(s,0,17), \tag{36}
\]
\[
 C_0=\sum_{s=1}^{12}\frac{s!}{18}L_{s+1}(s-1,0,18). \tag{37}
\]
Direct evaluation of the finite recurrences (16)–(22), using exact rational arithmetic, gives
\[
 \max_{0\leq t\leq16}G(t)=G(6)=\frac{341}{441}<\frac9{10}, \tag{38}
\]
\[
 \max_{0\leq j\leq16}G_0(j)=G_0(4)=\frac{541}{1050}<\frac9{10}. \tag{39}
\]
It also gives
\[
 C_1+5u_{13}
 =\frac{33167501663036036277491520814064645743}
 {37456474507093693098901091578183593750}
 <\frac9{10}, \tag{40}
\]
and
\[
 C_0+\frac{5u_{13}}2
 =\frac{7708263799436969382895449419535364626885341}
 {36262109049510970321139129724815573671875000}
 <\frac9{10}. \tag{41}
\]
These are merely evaluations of finite sums of rationals followed by cross multiplication. For orientation, the left sides of (40) and (41) are approximately \(0.885495\) and \(0.212571\), respectively.

We can now prove (14). By (24), with \(S=s+1,b=0,m=t,M'=M\),
\[
 F_{s+1}(s,t,M)\leq I_{s+1}(s,0,t,t),
\]
so the left side of (14) is at most \(G(t)\). For \(t\leq16\), use (38). If \(t\geq17\), split (34) at \(s=12\). For \(1\leq s\leq12\), (26) with \(q=17\) bounds the term by the corresponding term of \(C_1\). For \(s\geq13\), (29), with \(S=s+1,r=s,b=0\), gives
\[
 s!I_{s+1}(s,0,t,t)\leq \frac{s!2^s}{(s+2)^s}=u_s.
\]
Thus (33) and (40) give (14).

For (15), the second branch in (12) is absent at \(t=s+1\), because here \(S=s+1\). Hence
\[
 F_{s+1}(s,s+1,j)
 =\frac1{j+1}F_{s+1}(s-1,j+1,j+1),

after the first recursion step. Applying (23) gives the summand in (35), so the sum is bounded by \(G_0(j)\). For \(j\leq16\), use (39). For \(j\geq17\), split at \(s=12\). The first part is bounded by \(C_0\) using (25) and \(j+1\geq18\). For \(s\geq13\), (28), together with \(j+1\geq s+2\), gives
\[
 \frac{s!}{j+1}R_{s+1}(s-1,0,j+1)
 \leq\frac{u_s}{2}.
\]
Now (33) and (41) prove (15).

## 4. Transport from \((j-1)\)-part partitions to \(j\)-part partitions

For a finite set \(P\) of positive integers, let
\[
 m(P)=\min\{i\geq1:i\notin P\}, \tag{42}
\]
and let
\[
 P^+=\{x\in P:x>m(P)\}. \tag{43}
\]
Thus
\[
 P=\{1,2,\ldots,m(P)-1\}\,\dot\cup\,P^+. \tag{44}
\]
Define
\[
 \Phi(P)=\{1,2,\ldots,m(P)\}\cup \rho^{m(P)}(P^+). \tag{45}
\]

Suppose \(P\in\mathcal S(j-1,1,n)\), \(j\geq2\), and \(T_j\leq n\). Put \(s=m(P)\). Then
\[
 1\leq s\leq j-1, \tag{46}
\]
\[
 |P^+|=j-s, \qquad \sigma(P^+)+T_{s-1}=n. \tag{47}
\]
The upper set \(P^+\) has all its elements at least \(s+1\). Moreover,
\[
 \sum_{i=s+1}^{j}i+s\leq\sigma(P^+). \tag{48}
\]
Indeed, (48) follows by substituting (47) into \(T_j\leq n\) and using
\(T_j=T_s+\sum_{i=s+1}^j i\) and \(T_s=T_{s-1}+s\).

We need to know that \(\rho\) may be applied \(s\) times without creating an element at most \(s\). The following “excess” observation does this. If a nonempty set \(Z\) has \(j-s\) elements, all at least \(s+1\), and
\[
 \sum_{i=s+1}^j i<\sigma(Z), \tag{49}
\]
then \(\tau(Z)\geq s+2\). Otherwise \(\tau(Z)=s+1\), so \(Z\) would be the entire interval \([s+1,M(Z)]\). Its cardinality would force \(M(Z)=j\), making its sum exactly \(\sum_{i=s+1}^j i\), contrary to (49).

Starting from (48), induction shows that for \(0\leq i\leq s\), the set \(\rho^i(P^+)\) still has \(j-s\) elements, all at least \(s+1\), and
\[
 \sigma(\rho^i(P^+))+i=\sigma(P^+). \tag{50}
\]
At each stage before the last, the extra \(s-i>0\) in (48) gives the strict inequality (49), hence \(\tau\geq s+2\), and (3) applies while preserving the lower bound.

It follows from (45), (47), and (50) that \(\Phi(P)\) has \(j\) distinct positive elements and sum \(n\). Therefore
\[
 \Phi(P)\in\mathcal S(j,1,n). \tag{51}
\]

We now bound the weighted fibers of \(\Phi\). Fix \(Q\in\mathcal S(j,1,n)\). If \(P\) lies over \(Q\) and \(m(P)=s\), then (45) implies
\[
 \{1,\ldots,s\}\subseteq Q, \tag{52}
\]
\[
 P^+\in\{Y:\rho^s(Y)=Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s\},\ y\geq s+1\}, \tag{53}
\]
and, using (44),
\[
 \frac{P(Q)}{P(P)}
 =s!\frac{P(Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s\})}{P(P^+)}. \tag{54}
\]
For fixed \(s\), the map \(P\mapsto P^+\) is injective, because (44) recovers \(P\) from \(P^+\). Hence (53), (54), and (9) yield
\[
 \sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal S(j-1,1,n)\\\Phi(P)=Q}}
 \frac{P(Q)}{P(P)}
 \leq
 \sum_{s=1}^{j-1}
 \mathbf1_{\{1,\ldots,s\}\subseteq Q}\,
 s! f_s(Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s\};s+1). \tag{55}
\]

We claim that the right side is at most \(9/10\). There are two cases.

First suppose
\[
 Q=\{1,2,\ldots,j\}.
\]
Then
\(Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s\}=\{s+1,\ldots,j\}\), whose terminal-run bottom and maximum are \(s+1\) and \(j\). Therefore (13) and (15) give
\[
 \text{right side of (55)}
 \leq\sum_{s=1}^{j-1}s!F_{s+1}(s,s+1,j)\leq\frac9{10}. \tag{56}
\]

Now suppose \(Q\ne\{1,\ldots,j\}\). Let
\[
 s_Q=m(Q)-1,
 \qquad Q'=Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s_Q\},
 \qquad t=\tau(Q'),\quad M=M(Q'). \tag{57}
\]
The set \(Q'\) is nonempty, \(s_Q\leq j-1\), and every element of \(Q'\) is at least \(s_Q+2\), because \(m(Q)=s_Q+1\) is missing. Consequently
\[
 s_Q+2\leq t\leq M. \tag{58}
\]
The indicator in (55) vanishes for \(s>s_Q\). For \(1\leq s\leq s_Q\), adding back elements at most \(s_Q\) does not alter the terminal run or the maximum of \(Q'\); hence
\[
 \tau(Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s\})=t,
 \qquad M(Q\setminus\{1,\ldots,s\})=M. \tag{59}
\]
Using (13), (58), (59), and then enlarging the summation range,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \text{right side of (55)}
 &\leq\sum_{s=1}^{s_Q}s!F_{s+1}(s,t,M)\\
 &\leq\sum_{s=1}^{t-2}s!F_{s+1}(s,t,M)
 \leq\frac9{10}
 \end{aligned} \tag{60}
\]
by (14). Thus in all cases every weighted fiber satisfies
\[
 \sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal S(j-1,1,n)\\\Phi(P)=Q}}
 \frac{P(Q)}{P(P)}\leq\frac9{10}. \tag{61}
\]

Finally, sum (61) over all \(Q\in\mathcal S(j,1,n)\), divide the inequality for each \(Q\) by \(P(Q)\), and use (51) to partition the domain by the fibers of \(\Phi\). We obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 e_{j-1}(n)
 &=\sum_Q\sum_{\Phi(P)=Q}\frac1{P(P)}\\
 &=\sum_Q\frac1{P(Q)}
   \sum_{\Phi(P)=Q}\frac{P(Q)}{P(P)}\\
 &\leq\frac9{10}\sum_Q\frac1{P(Q)}
 =\frac9{10}e_j(n),
 \end{aligned}
\]
which proves (1).

## 5. Expansion of the generating function

Let \(a(n)\) denote the coefficient sequence in the question, so
\[
 a(n)=n![x^n]\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1-\frac{x^k}{k!}\right). \tag{62}
\]
Expanding the finite product by choosing either \(1\) or \(-x^k/k!\) from each factor gives
\[
 [x^n]\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left(1-\frac{x^k}{k!}\right)
 =\sum_{\substack{X\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\\sigma(X)=n}}
 \frac{(-1)^{|X|}}{P(X)}. \tag{63}
\]
The right side of (62) is indeed an integer: for each \(X\) occurring in (63),
\[
 \frac{n!}{\prod_{x\in X}x!}
 =\frac{(\sum_{x\in X}x)!}{\prod_{x\in X}x!}

a multinomial coefficient. Thus the floor used in the stated definition of \(A185895\) does not alter this rational value. Grouping (63) according to \(|X|\), we get
\[
 \frac{a(n)}{n!}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^j e_j(n). \tag{64}
\]

Let
\[
 m(n)=\max\{k:T_k\leq n\}. \tag{65}
\]
A strict partition into \(j\) positive parts has sum at least \(T_j\). One proof is to order its parts increasingly as
\(x_1<\cdots<x_j\); then \(x_i\geq i\), so their sum is at least \(1+\cdots+j\). Hence
\[
 e_j(n)=0\qquad(j>m(n)). \tag{66}
\]
Conversely, if \(1\leq j\) and \(T_j\leq n\), then
\[
 \{1,2,\ldots,j-1,\ n-T_{j-1}\}
\]
is a strict partition of \(n\) into \(j\) positive parts: the last part is at least \(j\). Therefore
\[
 e_j(n)>0. \tag{67}
\]
For \(n\geq1\), \(e_0(n)=0\). Combining this with (1) and (67), for every
\(1\leq j\leq m(n)\) we have
\[
 e_{j-1}(n)<e_j(n). \tag{68}
\]
(The case \(j=1\) follows from \(e_0(n)=0<e_1(n)\); the cases \(j\geq2\) follow from (1).)

We use the following elementary alternating-sum lemma. If
\[
 0\leq c_0<c_1<\cdots<c_m,
\]
with \(m\geq1\), then
\[
 0<(-1)^m\sum_{j=0}^m(-1)^jc_j\leq c_m. \tag{69}
\]
This follows by induction. For \(m=1\), it says \(0<c_1-c_0\leq c_1\). If it holds for \(m\), then
\[
 (-1)^{m+1}\sum_{j=0}^{m+1}(-1)^jc_j
 =c_{m+1}-(-1)^m\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^jc_j,

a quantity strictly between \(0\) and \(c_{m+1}\), because the second term is positive and at most \(c_m<c_{m+1}\).

Apply (69) to \(c_j=e_j(n)\), with \(m=m(n)\), using (66) and (68). Equation (64) gives, for \(n\geq1\),
\[
 0<(-1)^{m(n)}\frac{a(n)}{n!}. \tag{70}
\]
Since \(n!>0\),
\[
 (-1)^{m(n)}a(n)>0. \tag{71}
\]
For \(n=0\), directly \(a(0)=1\) and \(m(0)=0\), so (71) also holds. In particular, no term \(a(n)\) is zero, and its sign is exactly \((-1)^{m(n)}\).

## 6. When the sign changes

For \(n\geq1\), monotonicity of triangular numbers shows
\[
 m(n-1)\leq m(n)\leq m(n-1)+1. \tag{72}
\]
Indeed, every triangular number at most \(n-1\) is at most \(n\), proving the first inequality. If \(m(n)\geq m(n-1)+2\), then
\(T_{m(n-1)+1}<T_{m(n)}\leq n\). Since these are integers, this would give
\(T_{m(n-1)+1}\leq n-1\), contradicting the maximality of \(m(n-1)\).

Moreover,
\[
 m(n)\ne m(n-1)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_{m(n)}=n. \tag{73}
\]
If the two maxima differ and \(T_{m(n)}\leq n-1\), then \(m(n)\leq m(n-1)\), a contradiction. Conversely, if \(T_{m(n)}=n\) and the two maxima were equal, then the definition of \(m(n-1)\) would imply \(T_{m(n)}\leq n-1\), again a contradiction.

Finally,
\[
 T_{m(n)}=n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\text{ is triangular}. \tag{74}
\]
The forward implication is immediate. For the reverse implication, if \(n=T_k\), then \(k\leq m(n)\) by definition; strict increase of \(T_r\), together with \(T_{m(n)}\leq n=T_k\), forces \(m(n)=k\).

By (71), the signs of \(a(n)\) and \(a(n-1)\) are respectively
\((-1)^{m(n)}\) and \((-1)^{m(n-1)}\). In view of (72), these signs are opposite exactly when the two exponents differ, that is, exactly when \(m(n)\ne m(n-1)\). By (73) and (74), this occurs exactly when \(n\) is triangular. Since both terms are nonzero, having opposite signs is equivalent to
\[
 a(n)a(n-1)<0.
\]
Therefore, for every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
 a(n)a(n-1)<0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n=\frac{k(k+1)}2\text{ for some }k\geq0,
\]
as required.
